subject: Banking
title: Debt-to-Income Ratio
description: A quick, practical guide to Debt-to-Income Ratio.

hook.text: Your debt-to-income ratio tells a lender how much of your paycheck already goes to debt.

buildup.text: DTI is calculated by dividing monthly debt payments by gross monthly income. A $6,000 income with $2,400 in debt is 40%.

discovery.text: Lenders use DTI because credit scores don't show income. A high score with high debt-to-income still means risk.

twist.text: Student loan payments inflate DTI for young borrowers.

climax.text: DTI is the second gatekeeper after credit score. Both must pass for approval.

punchline.text: Keep debt below 43% of income. Both score and DTI must pass.

quiz.question: What DTI ratio typically disqualifies you from a mortgage?

details.summary: Debt-to-income ratio compares your monthly debt payments to your gross monthly income, and lenders use it as a key measure of your ability to handle additional debt. Most mortgage lenders require a DTI below 43 percent.
details.whyItMatters: DTI is often more important than your credit score for large loan approvals. A perfect credit score will not get you a mortgage if your existing debt payments consume too much of your income, making DTI a critical financial metric.
takeaways: DTI divides total monthly debt payments by gross monthly income
Most mortgage lenders require DTI below 43 percent
Student loans and car payments significantly impact DTI calculations

faq.question: What counts as debt in the DTI calculation?
faq.answer: Mortgage or rent, car loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments, personal loans, and child support all count. Utilities, insurance, groceries, and discretionary spending are not included in the standard DTI calculation.

faq.question: How can you lower your DTI quickly?
faq.answer: Pay off small debts entirely to remove their monthly payments. Increase income through raises, side work, or a higher-paying job. Refinance existing loans to lower monthly payments. Avoid taking on any new debt before applying for a loan.
